source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Assume lower RN staffing improves safety because fewer nurses reduce handoffs and therefore consistently decrease communication-related errors.","B":"Recognize lower or inadequate RN staffing as a patient-safety risk associated in observational evidence with missed care, adverse events, and mortality.","C":"Assume staffing does not influence patient outcomes when the number of occupied beds stays constant across the shift.","D":"Treat RN staffing only as a financial issue because clinical studies have not linked workload or staffing with patient-safety outcomes."}}
source_row.rationale: AHRQ PSNet summarizes evidence linking inadequate nurse staffing and workload with missed care, adverse events and mortality. NCSBN also classifies staffing/prioritization/quality activities under Management of Care.
source_row.source_detail: Introduction; Nursing Workforce Challenges and Patient Safety. AHRQ PSNet perspective published 2024-04-24; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Overview of Content — Management of Care, printed p.7: advocacy/client rights, prioritization, quality improvement, interdisciplinary collaboration, informed consent, legal scope and plan-of-care activities. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
source_row.source_name: AHRQ Patient Safety Network — Patient Safety Amid Nursing Workforce Challenges
source_row.stem: A nurse manager evaluates whether reducing registered-nurse staffing could affect patient safety. Which conclusion is most consistent with the evidence base?
